title: Moliere
full_review:
A playful and speculative exploration of a critical time in the life of France's great playwright and genius of comic satire, "Moliere" (Sony Classics) opens with 22-year-old actor and aspiring author Jean-Baptiste Poquelin (Romain Duris) thrown in debtor's jail, his theater troupe left languishing.

This entertaining and imaginative historical fiction fills in the blanks of what happens in the next several months, when Jean-Baptiste (who would change his name to Moliere, to avoid embarrassing his well-born family by his frowned-upon profession) mysteriously disappeared from Paris, only to return a transformed man and artist.

In the script's conceit, he is bailed out by a wealthy businessman, Monsieur Jourdain (Fabrice Luchini), who enlists Jean-Baptiste to teach him how to write a play -- and act in it, too.

Young Moliere is sworn to secrecy about the arrangement and is brought into the Jourdain household in the guise of a priest, charged with tutoring the family's youngest child in faith and morals. Moliere appropriates some church language for mildly comic purposes, and at one point improvises his version of the Our Father.

The ruse is meant to keep Madame Jourdain (Laura Morante) in the dark, because with his own play, Jourdain seeks to impress, and ultimately seduce, the Marquise Celimene (Ludivine Sagnier), who hosts an aristocratic salon where cruel wit reigns supreme. In his machinations, Jourdain is both aided and taken for a fool by the impoverished nobleman Dorante (Edouard Baer), who himself is scheming to marry off his son to Jourdain's daughter and thus attach himself to the family fortune.

Jourdain gives Moliere the name of Tartuffe, which is the first hint of another of the film's conceits. "Tartuffe" ("The Imposter") is, of course, the name of one of the playwright's celebrated later works.

His comic and ultimately morally redeeming adventures in the Jourdain household will give Moliere the raw material and inspiration for his greatest artistic creations in which comedy does justice to the complexities of the human soul. Director and co-writer (with Gregoire Vigneron) Laurent Tirard's film thus gives an amusing twist to the theme of art imitating life.

Sure enough, the sumptuous costume drama, accompanied by a beautiful score, starts off as a farce, making a delightful spectacle of the pretentiousness and hypocrisy of Dorante and Jourdain, whose acting lessons provide some of the film's comic highlights. Both duly get their comeuppance.

And Moliere ends up winning the heart of Madame Jourdain after she stumbles upon some pages of his passionate romantic writing discarded in her husband's study. But complications ensue.

The film contains some crude and sexual language, some liturgical and doctrinal irreverence, as well as mild sexual scenes of a somewhat romanticized adulterous relationship. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
